public_rationale: The Deep Research part holds. OpenAI said the tool was very compute-heavy and could struggle to tell authoritative sources from rumors. An independent February 2025 test found it often chose SEO-spam or company blogs over authoritative sources. The Operator part partly holds. Early testers found it slow and too error-prone to trust without supervision. But "rarely completes a task" goes too far. OpenAI's launch figures show the model behind Operator succeeded on 87% of WebVoyager tasks and 58% of WebArena web tasks, and on 9 or 10 of 10 trials for several everyday tasks. Only the harder full-computer benchmark (38%) and unfamiliar interfaces were below half. "Biggest, sexiest products" is rhetoric and was not scored.
limitations: Operator's success rates come from OpenAI and are not independently verified.
"Rarely" has no stated threshold, so the reading of it decides the Operator part.
There is no measured comparison of Operator's task times against a person's.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: More than two years into the generative AI boom, OpenAI's biggest, sexiest products are Deep Research, which spends a lot of compute to produce a poorly-cited research paper, and Operator, a compute-intensive application that rarely completes, in minutes, a task that would otherwise have taken you seconds.
conditions: more than two years into the generative AI boom

statement.excerpt: Let me put this in very blunt terms: we are more than two years into the generative AI boom and OpenAI's biggest, sexiest products are Deep Research — a product that dares to ask "what if you were able to spend a lot of compute to get a poorly-cited research paper," and Operator, a compute-intensive application that rarely completes a task in minutes that would otherwise have taken you seconds.

Deep Research: spend a lot of compute to get a poorly-cited research paper

our_interpretation: "Biggest, sexiest products" is rhetorical framing and is not scored.
The testable parts are: (a) Deep Research was compute-heavy and its citations and sources were of poor quality; (b) Operator was compute-heavy, slow, and rarely completed tasks.
Plain reading of "rarely completes": Operator failed at most of the tasks it attempted, so success was the exception, not the rule.
Period: the launch versions, from Operator's launch (2025-01-23) to the post date (2025-02-17).
criteria.support_condition: Evaluations from the period show that Deep Research often relied on weak or SEO-type sources and used heavy compute, and that Operator failed at most tasks and was slow.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evaluations from the period show Deep Research's sourcing was generally sound, or that Operator completed most of the tasks it attempted.

evidence.excerpt: achieving a 38.1% success rate on OSWorld for full computer use tasks, and 58.1% on WebArena and 87% on WebVoyager for web-based tasks.
evidence.explanation: Operator is a web agent, and on the two web benchmarks it succeeded on most tasks (58% and 87%). That cuts against "rarely completes." Only the full-computer benchmark is below half. These figures are vendor-reported.

evidence.excerpt: However, it still makes too many mistakes for human users to rely on it for important tasks without constant supervision.
evidence.explanation: Early testers found Operator slow and error-prone. This supports the general thrust of the Operator criticism, though not the claim that it rarely succeeds.

evidence.explanation: An independent evaluation of the launch version found that Deep Research often relied on SEO-spam and other weak sources. This supports "poorly-cited."
